claims_a: Refund requests spike in the two days after promo code launches.
Support categorizes post-promotion refund spikes as buyer's remorse patterns.
Refund approval skips payment method age verification to speed processing.
Most refund requests receive approval within 24 hours of submission.
Post-promotion refund spikes were tagged and shelved without root cause investigation.

output.connection: Post-promo refund spikes act as cover for payment-method-age fraud: because spikes are pre-tagged buyer's remorse and never investigated, refunds on newly-added payment methods can ride the wave and clear undetected.
output.mechanism: Approval skips payment method age checks, so a newly added (possibly stolen) payment method passes automatically. Because promo-driven spikes are already expected and shelved without root-cause work, any elevated share of new-payment-method refunds inside that window looks identical to ordinary buyer's remorse and draws no scrutiny.
output.testable_implication: Pull refund approvals from the most recent post-promo spike window and check what share used a payment method added in the prior 7 days, versus that same share in non-spike weeks.
output.needs: the claim supplies the specific co-occurrence of skipped verification, an unexamined recurring spike, and fast approval, which together create a blind spot no single fact would.

claims_a: Small transactions followed by refund requests within days correlate with accounts adding payment methods within 7 days.
Refund requests arrive within one week, but chargebacks hit processor 30-60 days later, delaying pattern detection.
Payment method recency within 7 days is the single strongest fraud signal for this pattern.
Refund justifications mask actual fraud until chargebacks scatter the signal across months of transaction logs.
Combining small purchase, quick refund request, and new payment method reveals fraud pattern clearly.
Overlapping IP ranges and similar phone numbers in account creation add weight but insufficient as solo signals.

output.connection: Because ground-truth fraud labels come from chargebacks lagging 30-60 days, any model or review process trained on those labels will systematically miss or misjudge the most recent 1-2 months of fraud.
output.mechanism: Chargeback confirmation is the only hard label; transactions from the last 30-60 days have not yet had time to chargeback, so they appear unlabeled or falsely clean, biasing any labeled dataset toward older fraud patterns and underweighting current ones.
output.testable_implication: Pull the fraud model's or reviewer's training/reference data this week and check the most recent labeled chargeback date; if it's more than 30 days old, flag the intervening window as unlabeled and re-score it using only the fast signal.
output.needs: the claim's specific 30-60 day chargeback lag combined with the claim that a faster signal already exists

claims_a: Judge context containing prior scores creates systematic upward bias of ~0.8 points on 10-point evaluation scale.
Removing prior score history from judge context eliminates upward drift and stabilizes blind rescores.
Updated protocol passes judge outputs with metadata only, maintains score log separately to prevent anchoring.
Regular rescoring of old batches detects and controls calibration drift in judges over time.
Eval judge prompt version v3 is locked; v1-v2 iterations will not be retroactively rescored.

output.connection: Historical v1-v2 scores stay inflated by the ~0.8-point anchoring bias forever, so any time-series or trend analysis spanning the v2-to-v3 boundary will show a spurious score drop that is a protocol artifact, not a real quality change.
output.mechanism: The bias came from prior-score context in judge prompts; v3 removes that context but explicitly won't rescore v1-v2 batches, so the old and new score distributions are non-comparable while sitting in the same log.
output.testable_implication: Blind-rescore a small sample of already-scored v2 items under the v3 protocol this week and diff against their logged v2 scores to quantify the exact discontinuity at the cutover.
output.needs: the claim's facts that the bias is quantified (~0.8 pts), v3 fixes it, and v1-v2 batches are explicitly excluded from retroactive rescoring

output.testable_implication: Before the October submission, check whether each cited prior-round score in the draft is followed by a sentence stating what it referred to and what was fixed.
output.needs: the claim supplies the loss of reviewer continuity plus the plan to cite raw numerical feedback

claims_a: The reminder system's relative timing (from last dose) causes daily drift of ~20 minutes, gradually pushing injection time later.
Adherence declined from 95% (weeks 1-3) to 72% (last 2 weeks) as injection time drifted from 6:15-6:45 AM to 7:30-7:50 AM.
Doses were missed entirely when reminders shifted past 8 AM (3 times in recent period).
The adherence decline appears driven by reminder timing drift rather than loss of motivation.
Switching from dose-relative to fixed clock-time reminders is the proposed solution to prevent drift.

output.connection: After each of the 3 full misses, the next reminder's anchor resets to whatever time the following dose actually happens, so post-miss drift may not follow the same predictable ~20 min/day pattern.
output.mechanism: The algorithm computes timing from 'last dose taken,' not a fixed schedule; a skipped dose removes the expected anchor point entirely, so the next interval starts from an arbitrary actual-dose time rather than the drifted-but-predictable prior slot.
output.testable_implication: Pull the logged reminder times for the 24-48 hours following each of the 3 missed doses and check whether drift resumed at roughly 20 min/day from the new anchor or jumped unpredictably.
output.needs: The claim's detail that timing is relative-to-last-dose and that 3 full misses occurred.

claims_a: Gateway operates on sleep schedule, listening only in 500ms wake windows at :00 and :30s, saving ~80% power vs continuous RX
Sleep schedule forces all downstream sensors to transmit precisely within the gateway's wake window
Sensors with internal oscillators drift significantly; within 48 hours, wake times misaligned ±200ms from gateway window
Clock drift caused 15-20% packet loss by day 3 before being diagnosed as timing issue, not RF noise
GPS-synced wake times with staggered offsets reduced packet loss to <2% and remained stable across resets

output.connection: The fix creates a hidden dependency on continuous GPS reception; any deployment location or condition that blocks GPS signal will let internal-oscillator drift resume and packet loss return to 15-20%.
output.mechanism: GPS sync only corrects drift while lock is held; sensors still run on free-running oscillators between syncs, so losing GPS reception removes the correction and drift reaccumulates exactly as before GPS was added.
output.testable_implication: Shield or disconnect GPS antennas on a few sensors for 48+ hours and check whether packet loss climbs back toward 15-20%.
output.needs: The claim supplies the pre-GPS drift timeline and the GPS fix's cross-reset stability, which together point to GPS-loss as the fix's untested failure mode.

output.testable_implication: Compare inventory turnover or stock-out rates between the control and treatment periods of the current weekly test before attributing any lift to the variant itself.
output.needs: The claim supplies both the newly adopted weekly cadence and the separately flagged inventory-turnover confound, but never links them as the same class of problem.

Log exact model checkpoint in metadata alongside temporal cutoff to ensure reproducibility.

output.connection: Other models trained on this same data source likely have similarly inflated random-split accuracy, since the leakage mechanism lives in the data, not in this one model.
output.mechanism: A 94% to 67% gap this large implies a generic leakage channel (e.g. near-duplicate or same-entity records scattered across time), and any model using this data source without a temporal cutoff shares that channel.
output.testable_implication: Rerun the last shipped model that used a random split on this same data source with the same time-ordered cutoff, and compare its reported accuracy to the temporal-split number.
output.needs: The magnitude and direction of the specific 94/67 gap as evidence that a systemic, data-level leakage mechanism exists, not just a one-off modeling error.

output.testable_implication: Pull this week's soil probe readings: confirm window IDs are sequential with no gaps (rules out sync drift), then compare a raw reading against a manual moisture check at the same spot to see if calibration drift is the separate, unflagged problem.
output.needs: The stated purpose of the Aug 22 schema change (detect sensor sync drift) plus the separately noted north-shelf soil probe drift needing recalibration.

claims_a: Fraudsters execute three or more card transactions within ten minutes; legitimate users rarely exceed two in that timeframe.

output.connection: The fixed 10-minute/3-transaction threshold implies a detectable evasion path: fraud rings that space charges just over 10 minutes apart never trigger flagging, and likely make up a disproportionate share of the missed 30%.
output.mechanism: Flagging fires only when 3+ transactions fall inside the same 10-minute window; any sequence with gaps of 11+ minutes between charges never crosses that trigger, no matter how many transactions occur or how high total velocity runs.
output.testable_implication: Pull inter-transaction time deltas for the 30% of confirmed-compromised cards that settled without being flagged, and check whether they cluster just above the 10-minute mark rather than being randomly distributed.
output.needs: the exact window and count threshold (3+ in 10 minutes) plus the reported 70% pre-settlement catch rate, which together define the boundary an adaptive fraudster would target.

claims_a: Weekly dose protocol specifies maximum total but not daily distribution requirements

Tracker records only weekly sum; cannot distinguish between clustered and spread doses
Weekly reset mechanism prevents tracking dose patterns across multiple weeks or months
Protocol permits taking double dose after skipping, with no constraint on clustering

output.connection: Skip-and-double clustering could span the weekly reset boundary: doubling at week's end and again at next week's start creates a short window of up to 4x normal dose, invisible to either week's tracker.
output.mechanism: Each week's total stays within the cap because the reset zeroes the count independently; the straddling window is never captured by any single week's sum, so a real short-term overdose leaves no record in either period.
output.testable_implication: Check the two or three days straddling the next weekly reset in the existing log for a skip-then-double pattern that would create this cross-boundary cluster.
output.needs: The claim supplies the weekly reset mechanism and the no-clustering-constraint on skip-and-double, which combine to produce this specific blind spot.
